claim_types: reports of a mice infestation and related repairs
evidence: The resident attached photos of mice droppings throughout the property.

Pest control contractors attended three times, confirmed moderate and then low-level infestation, confirmed droppings were present, laid bait, and recommended proofing holes in the kitchen and bathroom.
The landlord inspected the property and confirmed the kitchen components needed urgent updating due to their condition and said this was causing a mice infestation.
partial_case.facts: The resident lived in a 2-bedroom flat with her two children, complained of a mice infestation, droppings, related disrepair, and plastering/decorating issues following leaks, and reported household vulnerabilities. On 26 March 2024 she reported a mice infestation, holes allowing access, a complaint that the issue had existed since 2021, droppings throughout the property, vulnerabilities, mental health deterioration, unfitness for human habitation, and dissatisfaction with plastering and decorating after leaks. The landlord raised pest control works, issued complaint responses, and offered compensation. Pest control contractors attended in April and May 2024, confirmed infestation and droppings, and recommended proofing holes in the kitchen and bathroom. The resident later referred the matter to the Ombudsman because the proofing works had not been completed as agreed and she wanted increased compensation and learning from failures.

findings: Maladministration in the landlord’s handling of the resident’s reports of a mice infestation and related repairs.
Service failure in the landlord’s handling of the resident’s concerns about plastering and decorating.
Maladministration in the landlord’s handling of the complaint.
orders: Compensation of £1,010, comprising £800 for mice infestation response, £50 for plastering and decorating response, and £160 for complaint handling.
Learning order requiring the landlord to write to the resident about lessons learned and actions to prevent recurrence.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord initially responded quickly and arranged pest control treatment. However, it did not complete the recommended proofing of the property as agreed.
It failed to consider the reported vulnerabilities and impact on the household. Despite reports of mice droppings in the property it did not consider whether it was fit for human habitation.
The compensation offered was not proportionate to the length of time works were outstanding, and the impact on the household.
The landlord did not respond to the resident’s reports for 4 months. It provided a reasonable response at stage 2 but did not acknowledge its delay in doing so.

The landlord was late to acknowledge the complaint, and its stage 1 response did not assess its actions. It created an additional stage in its complaints process and did not acknowledge all its complaint handling failures or complete all its agreed actions.
It did not show due regard to its duties under Section 9.A of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 to ensure the property was fit for human habitation.
The landlord’s offer of redress was not proportionate to the failures identified and the impact caused to the resident and her children.
